Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Poll interval**: 15–20s is a reasonable default fixed interval; polling exactly on the minute to line up with the rollup job saves cycles but couples the client to a schedule note that says it can't be shortened, not guaranteed to stay put.
- **Skip-if-unchanged**: compare `computed_at` client-side (cheap, no server change) vs. have `api/metrics.js` return 304 via `If-None-Match`/`ETag` on `computed_at` (saves the 4KB payload but touches the server function).

Left out: backoff/pause when the tab is backgrounded (`visibilitychange`) — worth adding but a separate decision from the core polling mechanism.

WebSocket/SSE is out: `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions are killed at 10s, and instances freeze between invocations with no sticky routing — there's no way to hold a push channel open. So this has to be polling, and the good news is the data doesn't need anything faster: `jobs/rollup.md` says `rollup` only changes once a minute, on the minute, so sub-minute polling would just be hammering the DB for identical rows.

Build it as a client-side poll loop in `public/dashboard.js` replacing the load-once/click-only wiring: call `/api/metrics` every 30–60s, and re-render only if `computed_at` changed from the last response (cheap since the API already returns it). One thing worth deciding now rather than later: don't poll on an exact `:00` cadence for every client — that's the same instant the rollup job writes, so all open dashboards would hit `/api/metrics` at once right as the row is (maybe) mid-write. A few seconds of jitter or offset past the minute avoids that spike. Pausing the interval on `visibilitychange` when the tab's hidden is the next-level-down refinement, not required for correctness.

The core risk: on a timeout you don't know if the charge actually went through on the processor's side, so a naive retry can double-charge. Two things need to be true before you touch retry logic:

**Idempotency key per charge attempt.** Every charge request carries a key (Stripe, Adyen, Braintree all support this) that's stored with your local charge record before the call goes out. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a second charge — this is what makes retrying safe at all.

**Reconcile before retrying, don't just retry blind.** On timeout, first query the processor for that charge/payment-intent's actual status. If it succeeded, mark it succeeded locally — no retry. If it's genuinely unresolved or failed, then retry. This also needs to happen as a sweep job for charges left in "unknown" state, in case the reconcile call itself times out.

**Retry policy:** only for timeouts/5xx/network errors, not declines — a decline is a real answer, retrying it just annoys the customer. Exponential backoff with jitter, capped at 3-4 attempts, then fall to a final "needs manual/customer attention" state rather than infinite retry.

**UX fix, since that's the actual symptom:** move the charge off the request/response cycle into a background job, and have the checkout show "processing" while retry/reconcile runs, resolving to success or failed only once you have a real answer. That alone kills most of the "payment failed" reports, since today a timeout is presumably being surfaced as a hard failure when it's actually "unknown."

Which processor and is the charge call currently synchronous in the request path? That determines whether the queue/async piece is a small change or a bigger one.

The timeout itself is the bug in the UX, not the charge: a request timing out doesn't mean the charge failed, it means you don't know what happened. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; showing "payment failed" on a timeout is actively wrong when the charge may have gone through.

Design:
- Generate an idempotency key per logical charge attempt (tie it to the order/invoice ID, not the HTTP request) and send it on every retry, so the processor collapses retries into the original attempt instead of creating a second charge.
- On timeout, don't mark the payment failed — mark it "processing," enqueue a reconciliation check (poll the charge status or wait on the processor's webhook) before deciding success/fail.
- Retry only within that reconciliation path, same idempotency key, with backoff and a cap (e.g. 3 attempts) — never fire a fresh charge on retry.
- Update the customer once the real status resolves, instead of surfacing the timeout as the answer.

This forks hard on which payment processor you're on — idempotency keys are native in Stripe/Adyen/Braintree and that's the mechanism to build around. Which one are you using?

Recommendation: Postgres full-text search — a generated `tsvector` column over name + description, GIN-indexed, ranked with `ts_rank`, plus `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance — rather than standing up a separate search service.

The one fork that matters: catalog size and query volume. This approach holds up fine into the low millions of rows with normal traffic; past that, or once you need faceting/synonyms/semantic matching at scale, that's when Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Typesense earns its operational cost. Everything below "which datastore" — tokenization, ranking weights, autocomplete — is tuning, not architecture.

At 38k rows on Postgres 16, this doesn't need a search service — Postgres full-text search covers it. Add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name`/`description` with a GIN index, then query with `websearch_to_tsquery` ranked by `ts_rank`, exposed as a new `GET /search?q=` route alongside `routes/products.js`.

The one real fork: plain FTS (stemmed, word-based, fast) vs. adding `pg_trgm` similarity on top. Plain FTS misses typos and mid-word fragments; trigram catches those but has no relevance ranking of its own. Most product-search UIs want both — FTS for ranking, trigram as a fallback/boost for typo tolerance — but that's the layer I'd leave for a follow-up once you see real query logs, rather than building blind.

Left out: field-weighting (name matches ranked above description matches) and pagination of ranked results — both straightforward once the base index is in.

Direct-to-storage: have the client request a presigned upload URL from your app server, then PUT the file straight to S3/GCS/R2, and have the server process it (thumbnails, strip EXIF/GPS location data) asynchronously off a completion webhook or queue. This avoids routing multi-MB images through your app server.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Compress client-side or accept raw.** Phone photos run 3–12MB (or HEIC). Downscaling/re-encoding to JPEG in the browser/app before upload (canvas or a lib) cuts upload time and storage cost on flaky mobile connections; skipping it is simpler but pushes cost onto cellular uploads and server-side transcoding.
2. **Presigned direct upload vs proxy through your server.** Presigned URLs scale better and skip server bandwidth, but need CORS config on the bucket and a signed-URL endpoint; proxying is simpler to secure/validate but doubles bandwidth and ties upload speed to your server.

Everything past that — retry/resume for spotty connections, moderation, listing-photo ordering/limits — is next-level detail, not a fork.

Mirror the existing signed-URL pattern in `storage.js`, but for `PUT`: add an endpoint (e.g. `POST /:id/photos`) that returns a presigned PUT URL via `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })`, the client uploads the photo bytes straight to S3 with that URL, then the API stores the key with the already-existing `db.addPhotoKey`.

The fork that matters: don't route photo bytes through Express. `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at `1m` globally, on purpose — the payments team declined both a raise and a per-location override for PCI reasons — and a phone camera photo will routinely exceed that. Going direct-to-S3 sidesteps the limit entirely since S3 isn't behind that listener; the only things crossing nginx are small JSON calls to get the signed URL and to confirm the key. Bucket CORS already permits PUT from `market.example.com` (inherited from the admin tool's template), so no bucket-side change is needed either.

Left for the next level: key naming/prefix scheme, client-side validation before requesting the URL, and how multiple photos per listing get ordered.

Cache-aside with Redis: on a product page request, look up `product:{id}` (and any locale/currency variant in the key); on miss, hit the database, populate the cache, and return. That collapses the 900ms mostly to the DB call only on misses.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Invalidation**: if writes to products go through your own code, invalidate the key on write (accurate, no stale data); if products are edited out-of-band (admin tool, batch job, another service), you can't hook the write, so fall back to a TTL (a few minutes) instead.
- **Stampede protection**: once this is fast, a popular product's cache expiring will send every concurrent request to the DB at once. Use a short-lived lock or "stale-while-revalidate" (serve the expired value while one request refreshes it) to prevent that.

What's your write path for product data — through your app, or an external system?

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the read path: on a page request, check Redis by product key; on miss, hit the DB, write the result back with a TTL, then serve it. Invalidate explicitly from the write path (product update/delete deletes or refreshes the key) rather than relying on TTL alone — TTL-only gives you stale prices/stock for however long the TTL is, which is usually unacceptable for product pages.

The one fork worth deciding now: whether pages are personalized (price by user, regional stock, etc.). If not, you can cache the whole rendered page/fragment and even push it to a CDN edge; if they are, cache the DB query results/objects instead and keep rendering per-request.

Add request coalescing (single-flight) on cache miss so a cold key under concurrent load doesn't send N requests to the DB at once.

Left out: cache key design for locale/currency/experiment variants — that's the next layer down once you know how personalized these pages actually are.

Since there's no existing service here to key off, this is general practice, not something derived from your code.

Recommendation: enforce it at the gateway/proxy in front of `/v1`, not in application code — a request from the noisy client should get rejected before it consumes app resources. Use a token-bucket limiter keyed by client identity (API key or auth token, not IP, since IP is spoofable/shared), with capacity for normal burst behavior and a steady refill rate tuned to what a single well-behaved client actually needs.

The one fork that matters: if you run multiple gateway/app instances, per-instance in-memory counters won't catch a client spread across them — you need a shared store (Redis is the standard choice, via `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a Lua-scripted token bucket) so the limit is global. If you're single-instance, in-memory is fine and simpler.

Return `429` with a `Retry-After` header on rejection so well-behaved clients back off correctly.

Key on `client_id`, not IP — `routes/api.js` already notes clients share NAT addresses, so IP would throttle innocent neighbors of the noisy client while doing nothing to stop it if it rotates addresses.

Enforce in the existing auth middleware, right after `req.client` is resolved and before the Postgres calls: increment a counter in Redis (`redis.js` is already the only state shared across the 4 cluster workers and across boxes — `app.js` says explicitly that nothing in module scope is shared, so in-process counters would just let each worker allow its own quota). Do the check-and-increment as a small Lua script (`EVAL`) so it's atomic under concurrent requests from the same key, and use a token-bucket rather than a plain fixed window — a fixed window lets a client burst 2x at the boundary between windows, which is exactly the kind of hammering you're trying to stop. On limit exceeded, `res.status(429)` with a `Retry-After` header, before any DB work runs. Since `api_keys` already carries `plan`, key the bucket size/refill rate off `req.client.plan` so limits are per-tier, not global.

Left at the next level down: the actual limit numbers per plan, and whether to also keep a coarse per-IP cap as a secondary defense against key-less abuse (there is none right now — the 401 path runs before any counting).

The platform doc rules out the usual answer: WebSockets get a 501 at the edge, and even if they didn't, instances are frozen between invocations so nothing can hold a connection open past 10 seconds anyway. That leaves polling as the only option, not a choice among several.

Given that, and that `rollup` only changes once a minute on a fixed schedule (`jobs/rollup.md`), the design is just `dashboard.js`'s existing `load()` on a `setInterval`, roughly every 15-20s — often enough that a fresh minute doesn't sit stale for long, rare enough it stays well inside the endpoint's 4KB/30ms budget. Skip re-rendering when `computed_at` is unchanged from the last poll, so the UI doesn't flicker every cycle for no reason.

The one real fork: whether to also align polls to the minute boundary (e.g., poll at :05, :20, :35... past each minute) to shave the worst-case staleness down from ~20s to a few seconds, versus a plain fixed interval that's simpler but occasionally polls right before a rewrite. I'd start with the plain interval — the alignment gain is small and it adds a clock-skew edge case for little payoff.

Left out: retry/backoff on fetch failure and pausing the interval via the Page Visibility API when the tab isn't active — both cheap follow-ups, not part of the core design.

Poll, not push — WebSockets and SSE are both off the table here: `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions are killed at 10s, and instances are frozen between invocations with no shared memory, so nothing can hold a subscription open server-side anyway.

Given that, and that `rollup` only changes once a minute (`jobs/rollup.md`) with a `computed_at` stamp already in the response, the fix is client-side polling with a change check, not a new transport:

- In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the load-once/click-only wiring with `setInterval(load, ...)` at e.g. 15–20s (well under the 1-minute rollup cadence so staleness is bounded, but not so tight it hammers the function).
- Skip re-rendering when `computed_at` hasn't changed since the last fetch — `api/metrics.js` already returns it and sets `Cache-Control: no-store`, so each poll is a real 30ms/4KB read, cheap enough to just eat the cost rather than add conditional-GET logic.
- Pause the interval on `document.hidden` (visibilitychange) so backgrounded tabs don't keep polling.

That's the whole change: no new endpoint, no server process, no infra request. The only real decision is the poll interval, and 15–20s is the natural pick given the 1-minute rollup floor.

The fork is whether to retry synchronously inside the request or move it off the critical path — with timeouts already happening a few times a day, retrying synchronously just risks a second timeout and doubles the wait before the customer sees anything.

Better shape: on a timeout specifically (not a blanket catch-all — declines and insufficient-funds should still fail immediately), enqueue an async retry job and show the customer "processing" instead of "payment failed." The retry itself needs an idempotency key passed to the payment provider so a slow-but-actually-succeeded charge doesn't get double-charged on retry. Back off exponentially with a capped attempt count (e.g. 3 tries over a few minutes), and only surface a real failure once retries are exhausted — resolve via webhook/callback rather than having the customer poll.

The second fork is state tracking: you need a charge-attempt record (or reuse the payment provider's idempotency-key lookup) so a retry job checks current status before firing again, in case the original charge actually landed after the client-side timeout.

The actual bug isn't "no retry" — it's that `checkout.js:28-32` catches everything (including a timeout) and reports it as a decline, while `PROVIDER.md` explicitly says a timeout must be treated as **unknown**, never as failed. Retrying blind on top of that is what causes double charges.

Design:

1. **Mint an idempotency key per order, persisted before the first attempt** — e.g. an `idempotency_key` column set on the order row the first time `/pay` runs, not generated fresh inside `payments.charge()` per call. Every attempt for that order — a server-side retry, or the customer hitting "pay" again after seeing the current false failure — sends that same key.
2. `payments.charge()` sends `Idempotency-Key` and retries only on timeout/connection error (never on a 4xx decline, which is a real answer from the vendor), bounded (2-3 tries) with backoff. Because the key is stable, a retry after a real timeout either completes the original authorization or gets back the original charge — it can't authorize twice.
3. If retries exhaust, the state is still *unknown*, not failed. `checkout.js` needs a third order status (`payment_pending`/`unknown`) instead of collapsing into the current `catch → 502 "payment failed"`, and a reconciliation path (poll Cardstream for that idempotency key, or a webhook if one exists) to resolve it later rather than showing failure and inviting a resubmit that races the reconciliation.

The fork that actually matters is #1: where the key is minted. Persisted per-order before the first network call is what makes retrying safe at all; generating it inline per HTTP request would recreate the exact double-charge risk retries exist to avoid.

Postgres full-text search on a `tsvector` combining name (weighted higher) + description, with a GIN index — fast to build, no new infra, and good enough for keyword queries at moderate catalog sizes. Add trigram (`pg_trgm`) matching alongside it if you need typo tolerance.

The fork that matters: if catalogs are large (100k+ SKUs) or you want relevance ranking beyond keyword overlap (synonyms, "couch" matching "sofa"), that's when you'd reach for a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense for simplicity, Elasticsearch for scale) or embedding-based semantic search instead. Which of those is closer to your actual catalog size and quality bar?

The fork: whether you already run Postgres (or another relational DB) or need a standalone search service.

If Postgres, add a `tsvector` column combining name and description, weight name higher (`setweight(to_tsvector(name), 'A')`), GIN-index it, and query with `plainto_tsquery` on the user's words. Add `pg_trgm` if you want typo tolerance for short queries. This needs no new infrastructure and comfortably handles "type a few words, match name/description."

If you don't have a relational DB in the path, or you already know you'll need typo tolerance, faceting, or sub-100ms latency at higher scale, skip straight to a dedicated engine (Typesense or Meilisearch for ease of ops, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if you need it for other things too) — retrofitting that later means a second migration.

What's your stack — is there already a relational database in front of the product catalog? That decides which of the two to spec out. Relevance tuning (field weights, synonyms, ranking) is the next level down once the storage choice is made.

Direct-to-storage uploads: client requests a presigned URL/POST from your backend, then uploads the file straight to S3/GCS/Blob storage — never proxying multi-megabyte camera photos through your app server.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Compress before or after upload.** Resize/re-encode on the client (canvas downscale to ~2000px longest edge, JPEG ~80%) before the presigned upload — phone photos run 3-12MB and cellular upload is the real bottleneck, so shrinking client-side beats shrinking server-side.
2. **Sync vs async processing.** Don't generate thumbnails/variants in the request path. Have the storage write trigger a queue job that creates the sizes you need (thumbnail, listing-card, full) and flips the photo row from `pending` to `ready`. The listing save shouldn't block on image processing.

Data model: a separate `listing_photos` table (`listing_id`, `storage_key`, `position`, `status`) rather than an array column on the listing — lets uploads start before the listing is saved, supports reordering/deletion, and gives the async job somewhere to write status.

Left out: resumable/chunked upload for flaky mobile connections, EXIF orientation correction, and moderation/content scanning — worth a follow-up if any of those matter for this app.

Presigned direct-to-storage uploads: client asks your backend for a short-lived signed URL (S3/GCS/R2), uploads the file straight to object storage, then calls back to your backend with the returned key to attach it to the listing. Keeps large phone photos (often 5-15MB, sometimes 50MB+ on newer phones) off your app server entirely.

The one real fork: where you resize/strip EXIF orientation. Client-side (canvas/createImageBitmap before upload) cuts upload time and storage cost but adds complexity across every phone/browser quirk. Server-side (a Lambda/Cloud Function triggered on upload that generates thumbnails and a display size) is simpler and more consistent, at the cost of storing the original full-res file. Pick server-side first — simpler to ship, listings don't need sub-second upload feedback — and only push resizing to the client later if bandwidth/storage costs justify it.

Left out: multi-photo ordering/reordering UI state, upload retry/resumability on flaky mobile connections, and moderation/virus-scanning hooks — each is its own decision once the upload path above is in place.

The 900ms isn't missing a cache — it's that the CDN already in front of every request is caching 0% of it, because `middleware/security.js:8` sends `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on **every** route. That header was the 2024 audit fix for an `/account` page leaking between users, applied app-wide "to close the finding before the deadline" (per the comment) and never scoped back down. Per `CDN.md`, the CDN honors origin headers and platform eng won't add path rules for you — so headers are the only lever, and this bug is why it's unused.

**Fix:** split the policy. Keep `/account` on `no-store` (that's the real audit finding — user-specific data must never hit a shared cache). Give `/p` real cache headers, e.g. `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600`. That's safe because `routes/products.js` reads no session and states explicitly that price, stock, and copy are identical for everyone. This converts the 890ms of DB work (`db.js`'s own comments: 40ms + 600ms join + 250ms) into an edge cache hit for repeat requests — a bigger win than any app-level query cache, since it skips the app entirely.

**The one real fork:** `stockFor` (250ms) changes on a different clock than `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` (catalog edits, "a few times a day"). Two options:
- Bake stock into the same cached page. Simplest — one header change, done. Stock freshness is then tied to the page TTL (a few minutes of possible overselling-by-display).
- Split it out: cache the product/related markup at the edge with the longer TTL, serve stock from its own short-TTL path (or an app-side cache, e.g. Redis with a 10–30s TTL), fetched separately. More moving parts, but stock stays near-live regardless of page TTL.

Not covered: exact TTL tuning, purge-on-edit vs. TTL-only invalidation, app-level query caching — none of it matters until the header bug is fixed, since right now nothing reaches the edge cache at all.

Read `app.js`, `db.js`, `CDN.md`, the routes, and `middleware/security.js`. The picture:

- A CDN already sits in front of everything and honors origin `Cache-Control` — no path rules, no forced TTLs. Current hit rate: 0%.
- That's because `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` **app-wide**, applied after a 2024 audit finding on `/account` (a per-user orders page that leaked into an intermediary cache). It was slapped onto `/p` too, just to close the finding fast, and never revisited.
- `/p/:slug` is genuinely anonymous — no session read, same price/stock/copy for everyone. The 900ms is `relatedProducts` (~600ms, 4-table join) + `stockFor` (~250ms) + `productBySlug` (~40ms).

So the caching layer you need already exists. The build is: carve `/p` out of the blanket `no-store` and give it real `Cache-Control` (e.g. `public, max-age=...`), leaving `/account` exactly as locked-down as it is now. That turns edge hits into zero DB calls, not just a faster DB call.

Two decisions actually fork the design from there:

1. **Stock freshness.** It's the one field on the page that changes faster than "a few times a day." Bake it into the cached HTML with a short TTL and accept some staleness, or strip it out of the cached fragment and fetch it separately (short-TTL or uncached) so the expensive join can carry a long TTL independent of stock. Which is acceptable depends on how bad a stale "in stock" is for you — that's a product call, not an engineering one.
2. **Invalidation.** Catalog edits land in the admin tool a few times a day. Plain TTL (minutes) is probably fine and needs nothing beyond the header change. Only build purge-on-publish (calling the CDN's invalidation API from the admin save flow) if a few minutes of staleness after an edit is actually unacceptable.

Left out: cache-key/vary rules (should be trivial here since the route reads no cookies) and a DB-side cache (Redis/materialized view for the join) as a second layer once edge misses start mattering — not worth building before you know the edge hit rate.

Key constraint from the code: workers are clustered (4 per box, `app.js:7`) with no shared memory, and clients can share IPs behind NAT or use several IPs (`routes/api.js` comment) — so an in-process or IP-keyed limiter won't work. Redis is already the one thing every worker and box shares (`redis.js`), so build on that.

- **Key by `client_id`**, not IP. The auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves `req.client.client_id` and `req.client.plan` from the API key before your routes run — add the limiter right after that middleware, so it can key and set per-plan limits off data it already fetched.
- **Counter in Redis, not in process memory** — a Lua script (or `INCR` + `PEXPIRE NX`) per key like `rl:{client_id}:{windowStart}`, atomic so concurrent requests across all 4 workers × N boxes can't race past the limit. Fixed-window counter is enough; token bucket only matters if you need to smooth bursts rather than just cap them.
- On limit breach, `429` with `Retry-After`, before the `db.query` calls run — the point is to stop the noisy client's load from reaching Postgres, not just to report it.

The fork that actually matters: what happens if Redis is slow or down — fail-open (let requests through, matching current behavior) or fail-closed (block everyone). Given Redis is already a hard dependency for sessions, fail-open is the safer default so a Redis blip doesn't take down `/v1` entirely. Burst tolerance and per-plan limit values are tuning, not architecture — left out here.

Per-client token bucket enforced at the gateway/edge (nginx `limit_req`, Envoy, or Kong), keyed by API key rather than IP — keys survive NAT and shared-IP clients, IP doesn't. Store bucket state in Redis if `/v1` is served by more than one instance, so the limit holds across the fleet instead of resetting per-node. On breach, return `429` with a `Retry-After` header rather than silently dropping — well-behaved clients back off, badly-behaved ones you can rate-limit harder or block.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Limit granularity** — flat per-key limit vs. tiered by plan/contract. Flat is simpler and fixes today's problem; tiered matters once you have paying customers who need higher ceilings.
- **Enforcement point** — edge (stops the traffic before it costs you app/DB capacity, but blind to per-route cost differences) vs. app middleware (route-aware, can weight expensive endpoints higher, but the request has already consumed a connection/thread by the time you reject it).

Left out: burst sizing (bucket capacity vs. refill rate), and whether to complement this with per-IP or per-connection limits as a second layer against key rotation.

No sockets here — `PLATFORM.md` rules that out: connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions killed at 10s, no sticky routing, frozen instances between calls. Any "push" mechanism (WebSocket, SSE, long-poll) needs a connection nothing on this platform can hold open. So it has to be polling from `dashboard.js` against the existing `/api/metrics`.

The one thing worth designing rather than defaulting on: cadence. `rollup.md` says the table only changes once a minute, on the minute, and nothing else writes it — so a naive `setInterval(load, N)` either wastes most of its requests between writes or lags behind the write it's chasing. Scheduling each poll to land just after `:00` (using the `computed_at` you already get back to compute the delay to the next boundary) gets updates within a second or two of the real change with roughly 1/N the requests of a tight interval.

Left out: whether to skip re-render when `computed_at` is unchanged (at 4KB/30ms per `db.js`, probably not worth the extra conditional-request plumbing), and whether the "Refresh" button stays as a manual fallback or goes away.

WebSockets and SSE are both off the table here: PLATFORM.md says connection upgrades 501 at the edge, and even a long-poll would get killed at the 10s function limit with no shared memory between instances to resume from. Given the data only actually changes once a minute (`rollup.md`), the fix is client-side polling, not a push mechanism.

Build: in `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click/load-only wiring with `setInterval(load, 30000)` (or any interval under 60s) calling the existing `load()`. Keep `computed_at` doing the work it already does — compare the new value to the last-rendered one and skip the re-render if unchanged, so polling doesn't cause visible flicker every 30s for a value that only actually changes once a minute. `api/metrics.js` needs no changes; it's already cheap (30ms, 4KB, `no-store`) and stateless, which is exactly what repeated invocation on this platform wants.

One thing this doesn't give you: sub-minute freshness. Since `rollup` is only written once a minute by a schedule tied to the finance close window, no amount of client cleverness gets you closer to real-time than that.

Treat a timeout as "unknown," not "failed" — retry the same charge using an idempotency key tied to the order, with a couple of bounded attempts and backoff, before ever showing the customer anything.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Idempotency key scope.** Key it to the order/attempt (not regenerated per retry), so retries — and duplicate clicks — resolve to the one charge instead of risking a double-charge when the original request actually went through on the processor's side despite the timeout.
2. **Sync vs. async retry.** Retry inline in the same request (2-3 attempts, short backoff, customer sees a spinner) if your latency budget is under ~10s total; otherwise return "processing" immediately and retry from a background job/queue, updating the order via the processor's webhook when it resolves — necessary if the processor's own timeout means the charge could complete minutes later.

Left out: reconciliation for charges that succeeded after the client stopped waiting (a webhook handler matching on idempotency key that finalizes the order even with no one watching), and a retry cap/dead-letter path so a genuinely declined card doesn't loop forever.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

**1. Never blindly resubmit — reconcile first, then retry with the same idempotency key.** A timeout is ambiguous: the processor may have gone through despite the response never arriving. Retrying with a fresh charge request risks double-charging. Generate an idempotency key up front, persist it with the charge attempt, and on retry either query the processor for that key's actual status or resubmit with the *same* key so the processor de-dupes it server-side. Only retry timeouts and other transient errors (network failure, 5xx) — never retry a hard decline (insufficient funds, fraud block), since those are real answers not lost ones.

**2. Move the retry off the request path and give the customer a "processing" state instead of "payment failed."** The reason the customer sees "payment failed" today is presumably that a timeout is being treated as a terminal failure synchronously. Instead: charge gets a state machine (`pending → processing → succeeded/failed`), the initial timeout moves it to `processing` and enqueues a background retry job with backoff (e.g. a few attempts over a couple minutes), and the customer sees a non-final status until retries are exhausted. Only surface "payment failed" after the last retry fails or a hard decline comes back.

Left out at this altitude: the backoff schedule and max attempt count, how failed-after-retries gets alerted/reconciled against the processor's own webhook events (which should also update the state machine, since a late webhook can resolve the ambiguity before your retry even fires), and whether webhooks alone might replace polling-based reconciliation.

Postgres full-text search is the right default: a generated `tsvector` column combining name + description, GIN-indexed, queried with `websearch_to_tsquery` and ranked with `ts_rank`. It handles "a few words" queries well and needs no new infra if the catalog already lives in Postgres.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Scale/typo-tolerance.** Postgres FTS is fine up to roughly low-millions of rows and doesn't need to be fast-fast. If you need fuzzy/typo-tolerant matching, faceted filters, or sub-100ms latency at bigger scale, that's when a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) earns its keep — at the cost of a sync pipeline (CDC or scheduled reindex) to keep it current with the DB.
- **Keyword vs. semantic.** Plain keyword FTS covers literal name/description matches; if users type vague or conceptual queries ("cozy winter blanket") that don't share words with the catalog text, you'd add embedding-based semantic search — which means a vector store and an embedding pipeline, real added cost for a v1.

Left out: ranking/synonym tuning and autocomplete — worth designing once the base index choice is picked.

Recommendation: presigned direct-to-storage upload, not a proxy through your app server. The client (phone) requests a signed PUT/POST URL from your API, uploads the image straight to S3/GCS/R2, then confirms completion back to the API, which records the photo row against the listing. This keeps multi-MB camera images off your app servers.

The two decisions that actually fork the design:

- **Resize before or after upload.** Phone cameras produce 3-10MB, 4000px+ images with EXIF rotation quirks. Resizing client-side (canvas/`createImageBitmap`, cap to ~1600px long edge) before upload cuts upload time and storage cost dramatically, but adds client complexity and a slower/lower-power-device tax. If you skip that, do it server-side via a queued job triggered on upload-complete, so the request that returns to the user isn't blocked on processing.
- **Sync vs. async availability.** Photos won't be listing-ready the instant the bytes land — thumbnails, format conversion, maybe moderation. Model the photo as having a status (`pending`/`ready`/`failed`) rather than assuming it's usable the moment upload finishes; the listing UI polls or gets pushed the state change.

Left out at this depth: retry/resume for flaky mobile uploads, storage key/CDN layout, and image moderation — worth a follow-up once the above is settled.

Two decisions actually shape this:

1. **Upload path**: direct-to-object-storage via a presigned URL (client uploads straight to S3/GCS/R2), not proxied through your app server. Phone photos run 3–10MB (HEIC often more); routing that through your server multiplies bandwidth/memory for no benefit. Your server's job shrinks to issuing the presigned URL and recording the object key once the client confirms the upload finished.

2. **Client-side downsizing before upload**: the mobile network is the bottleneck, not storage. Resize/re-encode on-device (canvas or native) to something like 1600–2048px longest edge and convert HEIC to JPEG *before* the upload starts. That cuts upload time on cellular and keeps your backend from needing a synchronous resize step blocking listing save.

Given flaky mobile connections, plan for resumable/chunked upload (S3 multipart or tus) rather than a single PUT that dies at 90% and forces a full retry.

Thumbnailing, CDN delivery, photo ordering, and EXIF-orientation handling are a level down from these two calls.

That alone should take most requests from ~900ms to single-digit ms.

If not (e.g., inventory count), you need event-driven invalidation — bust the cache key on write instead of waiting for TTL, which means every write path that touches that product has to know to invalidate it.

Left out: cache stampede protection (locking or jitter on expiry so concurrent misses don't all hit the DB at once) and whether to cache the raw query result vs. the fully rendered page fragment — that second one depends on your stack, which I don't have here.

Nearly all of that 900ms is three queries in `db.js`: `productBySlug` (~40ms), `relatedProducts` (~600ms), `stockFor` (~250ms) — called from `routes/products.js:10-13`. None of it is per-user; the route reads no session.

Stock changes with every order, so caching the whole page at that same long TTL means selling out-of-stock items. Two ways to resolve it: cache the whole page short (30-60s) and accept brief stock staleness, or split stock out of the cached fragment (separate fast endpoint, uncached or very-short-TTL) so the expensive, stable 640ms gets a long TTL and stock stays live. Left out: per-tier limits (some clients get higher quotas), and burst-size tuning (bucket capacity vs. refill rate) — that's calibration once the mechanism's in place, not a fork in the design.

Use an atomic Redis op (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`, or a small Lua script if you want token-bucket smoothness instead of fixed-window edge bursts) keyed by `ratelimit:{client_id}`, with the limit picked from `req.client.plan`.

**Why not push:** `PLATFORM.md` rules out WebSockets (connection upgrades 501 at the edge) and SSE/long-lived connections (instances freeze between invocations, no sticky routing to resume a stream on). Moving off the platform was already declined. Left out: pausing polling on `visibilitychange` for backgrounded tabs, and fetch error/retry handling — both small, neither forks the design.

Push-based updates (WebSocket/SSE) are off the table here: `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge and instances are frozen between invocations, so nothing can hold a subscription open. This has to be polling from the browser — the fork is what kind.

**Recommendation:** replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with a poll loop that's aligned to the rollup's actual cadence rather than polling blindly. `jobs/rollup.md` says the table is rewritten once a minute, on the minute, and is otherwise byte-identical — so schedule each fetch for a few seconds after the next `:00` (computed from the `computed_at` you already get back), not a fixed setInterval from page load. That's ~1 request/minute instead of 2+, and it usually lands right after the fresh write instead of racing it.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Cadence: aligned-to-minute vs. fixed short interval.** Aligned is cheaper and matches a schedule the doc says won't shorten. Fixed interval is more robust if that ever changes, but you'd be paying for robustness against a constraint the doc says is fixed by finance close.
2. **Where staleness is detected: client-side vs. conditional request.** `/api/metrics` already returns `computed_at`; comparing it client-side before re-rendering (skip DOM update if unchanged) is enough. Standing up ETag/If-Modified-Since on top of a 10-second serverless function that already does a 30ms/4KB query would be added plumbing for no real savings.

Left out as pure implementation detail, not a fork: pausing the loop on `visibilitychange` when the tab is hidden, and backoff behavior if a fetch fails.

The fork that matters: a timeout is *ambiguous*, not a failure — the charge may have gone through on the processor's side. Retrying blindly without protection risks double-charging the customer.

- **Idempotency key**: generate one per charge attempt (e.g. `order_id` + attempt epoch), reuse the same key on every retry. Stripe/most processors dedupe on it, so a resent request either returns the original result or safely creates one charge.
- **Check before retry**: on timeout, query the processor for that idempotency key's status before resending — if it confirms no charge or a genuine failure, retry; if it confirms success, treat it as paid.
- **Only retry retryable errors**: timeouts/network errors/5xx, not declines — a decline is definitive and retrying it just produces the same "payment failed" with wasted attempts.
- **Sync vs async**: a couple of inline retries with short backoff (~1-2 attempts, sub-second) if timeouts are usually transient; if they can hang for real, move to a background job with exponential backoff, mark the order "processing," and update the customer async (webhook/poll) instead of blocking the request.

Depth I'm skipping: dead-letter/alerting after max retries, and reconciliation jobs for charges left stuck in "processing."

Two things matter most here, since a timeout means you don't actually know if the charge succeeded:

- **Idempotency key on the charge request**, generated once per attempt and reused on every retry. Without this, "retrying" a timed-out charge risks double-charging the customer if the original request actually went through on the processor's side.
- **Reconcile before you retry, don't just retry.** On timeout, query the processor for that idempotency key's status (or wait for its webhook) first. If it shows succeeded, treat it as success; only fire a new attempt if it's genuinely unresolved/failed.

The fork: do this **inline** (retry synchronously within the same request, a couple of quick attempts with backoff, before responding to the customer) or **async** (return "processing," enqueue a job that retries with backoff and idempotency key, then notify/update the UI once resolved). Async is safer for payments — it doesn't block the checkout request on a flaky processor and gives you a natural place to cap retries and alert on exhaustion — but it means the customer doesn't get an instant answer, so the UI needs a "processing" state instead of an immediate result.

Also worth separating: retry only on transport-level failures (timeout, 5xx, connection reset), never on a real decline — retrying a decline just wastes attempts and won't change the outcome.

Two forking decisions, then a pick:

**Where the index lives.** If the catalog is already in Postgres/MySQL and catalog size is under ~1M rows, use the database's built-in full-text search (Postgres `tsvector`/`tsquery` with a GIN index over name+description, weighted so name matches rank above description matches) — no new infra, no sync lag. If you need typo-tolerance, faceting, or the catalog is large/growing fast, use a dedicated engine (Meilisearch/Typesense for simplicity, OpenSearch/Elasticsearch for scale) with the catalog mirrored into it.

**How the index stays fresh.** Query-time search against the live table only works with Postgres FTS. A dedicated search engine needs a separate index kept in sync via either an outbox/CDC pipeline (reliable, more moving parts) or synchronous writes on product create/update (simpler, but risks drift on failures).

Pick: start with Postgres FTS — cheapest to ship, and the search box just becomes a `WHERE search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery(...)` clause with a rank-order `ORDER BY`. Revisit a dedicated engine only once relevance complaints or catalog size force it.

Left out: autocomplete/typeahead, synonyms/typo-tolerance, and filtering by category/price — next level down once the basic query path is settled.

Recommendation: if the catalog already lives in Postgres, start with Postgres full-text search — a `tsvector` column combining name + description, a GIN index, and `ts_rank` for ordering. It ships with zero new infra and handles "a few words" queries fine up to a few hundred thousand products.

Two things actually fork this:

1. **Catalog size / relevance bar.** If it stays under ~100k–500k products and typo-tolerance isn't critical, Postgres FTS is enough. Past that, or if you need fuzzy matching, faceting, or fast relevance tuning, move to a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) — better ranking and speed, but now you're running and syncing a second data store.
2. **Sync strategy**, only if you pick the dedicated-engine path: index on write (product save triggers an upsert to the search index) vs. periodic batch reindex. On-write is more complex but keeps search fresh; batch is simpler but has staleness lag.

Everything below that — tokenization/stemming config, autocomplete, typo distance thresholds — is tuning, not architecture.

- **Resize before or after upload.** Do it client-side first — phone photos run 3–10MB at 4000×3000, and shipping that raw wastes mobile data and slows the seller's flow. - **Photo record lifecycle.** Create the photo row (status: pending) before the upload starts, not after, so the presigned URL is tied to a real ID and a failed/retried upload doesn't create duplicates. Flip it to `active` on the client's confirm call.

- `storage.js` (storage.js:14) already signs `PUT`, and the bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` — added for exactly this, never wired up.
- `db.js` already has `listings.photo_keys` (text array) and `addPhotoKey(id, key)` — column's been sitting empty since there's no write path.

Cache the DB query results in Redis, keyed by product ID, with a short TTL (minutes) plus explicit invalidation on product writes — not a CDN/full-page cache, since product pages usually have per-user elements (cart state, personalization) that break page-level caching.

Two decisions that actually fork this:

- **Invalidation**: event-driven (bust the key on the write path when a product updates) vs. pure TTL. Event-driven keeps data fresher but couples the write path to cache logic; TTL-only is simpler but serves stale prices/stock for up to the TTL window. Pick TTL-only first — simpler, and 900ms→~5ms is the win regardless of a few minutes of staleness — then add event-driven invalidation only for fields where staleness actually causes problems (price, stock).
- **Stampede protection**: a popular product's cache expiring under load can send a burst of requests through to the DB at once. Use single-flight (first request to miss fetches and populates, others wait) or serve-stale-while-revalidate to avoid that.

Left out: cache warming, multi-region cache topology, and whether to cache at the query level vs. a higher-level "assembled page data" object — those matter once you know your read/write ratio and DB query shape, which I don't have here.

The 900ms isn't a caching gap you need to build — it's one you need to unblock. The CDN (CDN.md) already fronts every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends, but `middleware/security.js` forces `no-store` on *every* route, applied app-wide after the 2024 audit finding about the `/account/orders` leak. `/p/:slug` (routes/products.js) is anonymous and identical for all users — it never should have been included.

Fix: move that `no-store`/`Pragma` block off the global `app.use(security)` and onto `/account` only, then have `/p` send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<a few hours>` to match how often catalog rows actually change. That alone lets the CDN start serving `relatedProducts` (~600ms) and `productBySlug` (~40ms) from the edge — no new cache layer to build.

The one real fork is `stockFor` (~250ms): it's baked into the same page but changes on every order, far faster than the catalog. Either accept some staleness and pick a short page TTL (~5–15min), or split stock out of the cached shell into its own short/no-cache request so inventory freshness isn't chained to catalog TTL. Purge-on-admin-edit (surrogate keys/cache tags) is the next layer down if staleness turns out to matter.

- **A timeout is being told to customers as "failed"** (`checkout.js:31`), but `PROVIDER.md:11` says the vendor's own guidance is to treat a timed-out charge as **unknown**, never failed. That's a mislabeling bug independent of retries.

- **Async** — on timeout, save the idempotency key, mark the order `processing`, return that to the customer immediately, and retry from a background job/queue until Cardstream gives a definitive answer, then update the order and notify the customer (webhook or poll).

Given this is "a few times a day," I'd pick inline/sync: reuse the idempotency key, retry a couple of times in-request, and if still unresolved, store the order as `processing` (not `failed`) rather than inventing a queue and notification path for something this rare. Use an idempotency key per charge attempt (generated client-side or at order creation, sent with every retry of that same logical charge) so retries can never double-charge — this is the fork that matters most, since a timeout means you don't know if the processor actually completed the charge.

On timeout: don't blindly retry. First re-query the charge status (via the idempotency key or a status lookup) to see if it actually succeeded; only submit a new attempt if it didn't. Do this in a background job with backoff (e.g. 3 attempts over ~30s), not inline in the request that's holding the customer's browser.
